raw_case_text: The present case report is about a 40-year-old male patient who presented with high-grade fever associated with chills, jaundice vomiting and abdominal pain for 4 days. There was no history of cough, burning micturition, diarrhea or altered sensorium. On physical examination, he was alert, but febrile (103  Fahrenheit) with mild jaundice. He gradually became drowsy 3 days after admission. Systemic examinations were within the normal limit except epigastric tenderness and abdominal distension with normal bowel sounds. Laboratory investigations revealed hemoglobin - 10.2 g/dl, total leucocyte count - 15,100 (with Neutrophil - 87%) and platelets - 2.75 lacs/cu.mm. Peripheral blood smear revealed ring forms of P. falciparum. Immunochromatographic test for P. falciparum histidine-rich protein 2-based assay was strongly positive. Liver function testing showed serum Total Bilirubin - 4.4 mg/dl (Direct Bilirubin - 2 mg/dl) and serum aminotransferases and alkaline phosphatase were within normal limits. Serum amylase was 525 IU/L and serum lipase was 250 IU/L. Renal function and electrolytes were normal (Serum urea - 32 mg/dl, serum creatinine - 1.2 mg/dl, serum sodium - 140 meq/L and serum potassium - 4.1 meq/L). Urine and blood cultures came out to be sterile. Serum calcium was 9.2 mg/dl and fasting lipid profile was within the normal limits (cholesterol - 170 mg/dl, triglycerides - 103 mg/dl, high density lipoprotein - 36 mg/dl, low density lipoprotein - 114 mg/dl and very low density lipoprotein-20 mg/dl). Chest X-ray was normal and abdominal X-ray showed "Ileus" without air-fluid levels. Ultra sonography abdomen demonstrated an edematous, enlarged pancreas with minimal fluid in the peritoneal cavity. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen revealed edematous, enlarged pancreas with multiple fluid collections around pancreas and in the peritoneal cavity [Figure 1]. A diagnosis of severe falciparum malaria with acute pancreatitis (Grade E, CT severity index-4) was made and treatment was initiated with intravenous artesunate. There was marked improvement in his clinical symptoms in next 48 h. Acute pancreatitis was managed with analgesics, hydration and supportive therapy. Ryle's tube was initially instituted for bowel rest. After 3 days, his spikes of fever came down. From day 5, he started tolerating oral feeds. His pain abdomen and jaundice subsided after 8 days. He was discharged after a hospital stay of 12 days. On his follow-up visit, 2 months later, he was symptom free and doing well.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male presenting with a 4-day history of high-grade fever of 103 F, chills, jaundice, vomiting, and severe epigastric pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with high-grade fever accompanied by chills, jaundice, vomiting, and abdominal pain that started 4 days prior to admission. Three days into hospitalization, he developed progressive drowsiness and worsening abdominal distension. He denied respiratory, bowel, or urinary symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Denied prior history of gallstones, alcohol use, pancreatitis, or abdominal surgery.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, vomiting, abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and jaundice. Negative for cough, dysuria, diarrhea, or rash. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 103 F. Alert initially, progressively drowsy on hospital day 3; mild scleral icterus present. Abdomen: Epigastric tenderness and abdominal distension with audible normal bowel sounds; no peritoneal rigidity. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological examinations were otherwise normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 10.2 g/dL, total leukocyte count: 15,100/mm3 (neutrophils: 87%), platelet count: 2.75 lacs/cu.mm (275,000/mm3). Serum total bilirubin: 4.4 mg/dL (direct bilirubin: 2.0 mg/dL), serum aminotransferases and alkaline phosphatase: Within normal limits. Serum amylase: 525 IU/L, serum lipase: 250 IU/L. Serum calcium: 9.2 mg/dL. Renal function and electrolytes: Serum urea: 32 mg/dL, serum creatinine: 1.2 mg/dL, serum sodium: 140 mEq/L, serum potassium: 4.1 mEq/L. Fasting lipid profile: Total cholesterol: 170 mg/dL, triglycerides: 103 mg/dL, HDL: 36 mg/dL, LDL: 114 mg/dL, VLDL: 20 mg/dL. Blood and urine cultures: Sterile. Chest X-ray: Normal. Plain abdominal radiograph: Ileus without air-fluid levels. Abdominal ultrasonography: Edematous, enlarged pancreas with minimal free peritoneal fluid.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan: Edematous, enlarged pancreas with multiple peripancreatic and peritoneal fluid collections, consistent with acute necrotizing/exudative pancreatitis (Balthazar Grade E, CT Severity Index: 4).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum infection complicated by acute interstitial edematous/exudative pancreatitis (Grade E, CT severity index 4) and hyperbilirubinemia.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood smear demonstrated ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum; immunochromatographic assay for Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein 2 (PfHRP-2) was strongly positive. Hypertriglyceridemia, gallstones, alcoholism, and bacterial sepsis were excluded.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with intravenous artesunate targeting falciparum parasitemia. Acute pancreatitis managed with bowel rest via nasogastric (Ryle's) tube decompression, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, and analgesia. Marked clinical improvement occurred within 48 hours; fever spikes resolved within 3 days, oral feeding was resumed on day 5, and abdominal pain and jaundice completely resolved by day 8. Discharged on hospital day 12 with full recovery and asymptomatic status at 2-month follow-up.
